findings.note: Roslyn impact reports this direct internal edge. It preserves the mapped generic path and reaches the batch overload.
The single-item workflow calls the single-item overload, distinct from Save(IEnumerable<T>).
This is the reported batch path into the filtered enumerable overload.
Mapped imports call SaveMapped; its implementation then invokes the enumerable Save overload.
OrderBatchFactory is a possible workflow construction point around imports; it does not implement repository persistence.
Create constructs the workflow from a supplied repository, making it relevant to the managed workflow architecture but not the filtering defect.
Register adds a transient workflow factory to WorkScope; runtime registration/activation is not established by this source signal.
The registration resolves OrderRepository<Order> before creating the workflow; this wiring does not explain row omission.
The factory is invoked from the registration delegate; this is candidate construction evidence, not a resolved runtime edge.

The bridge declares a managed ref class, constructs OrderImportWorkflow<Order^>, and invokes ImportBatch. This is a possible boundary path, but it is not compiler-resolved managed evidence; the bridge passes nullptr and an empty list in this analysis fixture.
ISessionFactory is held and constructor-injected in a separate legacy data-access class; no source edge connects it to the managed OrderRepository<T> overload.
The legacy data-access wrapper receives its NHibernate factory through its constructor; no construction or managed workflow relationship is established.
The legacy wrapper opens a session and calls SaveOrUpdate on OrderEntity. It is a separate persistence path and does not establish the cause of the in-memory managed batch filter.
The legacy wrapper begins and commits an NHibernate transaction around one entity save; no relation to the affected managed repository is established.
The legacy Framework project declares NHibernate 5.5.2; dependency metadata alone does not connect it to the managed project.
MFC dynamic creation is present in the native view. It is a framework boundary lead, not evidence that MFC causes omission in the managed repository.
The message-map block surrounds the batch command handler; macro dispatch is not a resolved C# call edge.
The native view derives from CFormView and is part of the possible UI boundary; it does not establish persistence behavior.
The view declares MFC dynamic creation metadata; runtime creation is not established.
This maps the legacy OrderEntity, whereas the affected managed repository stores T in its local list; mapping activation and any relation are unproven.
A legacy NHibernate session-factory configuration exists, but its activation and relationship to the managed workflow are not established.
The project targets .NET Framework 4.7.2 and is separate from the managed net10.0 repository project; it is boundary context, not a proven cause.
This check invokes ImportBatch with one retry-marked and one ordinary order and asserts that both are saved; the required independent managed check runs this file.

limitations: BrownPants impact.md provides four direct Depth 1 managed edges; test-caller rows at greater depth are intentionally represented by the test-identification finding, not as managed-call findings.

MFC and C++/CLI relationships are lexical boundary candidates, not compiler-resolved calls. The bridge's sample invocation uses a null repository and an empty list, so it does not demonstrate runtime execution of the reported defect.

The legacy NHibernate entity, session, mapping, configuration, and .NET Framework project have no established relationship to the managed OrderRepository<T> path; activation and transitive runtime behavior are unknown.
The managed source identifies the retry predicate as the row omission cause; no ORM or native artifact was changed.
